author: DreemExtended
text:
Here’s how we used SMS + voicemail to get clients for our AI UGC agency.

We started pretty simple.

First, we went looking for ecom brands that were already running ads.

The reason was obvious. If they’re already spending money on ads, they probably need new creatives constantly.

So we researched a bunch of brands, built a list of around 500 to 1,000 of them, and collected their business contact info.

Then instead of sending some generic:

“Hey, we offer AI UGC. Interested?”

We actually gave them a reason to reply.

One of the messages we tested was:

“Hey, I looked you guys up and saw you’re running Facebook ads. I checked out some of your creatives and decided to create some AI UGC content for you.

If you don’t mind, I’d love to send it over.”

We tested a few different angles too.

Direct pitch.

Free creative.

Free trial.

Free resource.

Different scripts, different offers, different approaches.

We also combined SMS with voicemail drops instead of relying on just one channel.

And whenever someone actually replied positively?

We called them.

No 3 day texting back and forth.

If they liked the free trial, we’d get them on a call and continue from there.

If another offer was getting better responses, we’d push that one harder.

That’s really the lesson here.

SMS wasn’t some magic button.

The actual advantage was being able to test different offers quickly, see what people responded to, and then put more energy behind the thing that was working.

Find the right people.

Give them something relevant.

Test different angles.

Follow up fast.

Then scale the winner.

DM me “SCALE” if you want us to run this same system for your business.

author: WasimShips
text:
I've watched founders hit $10K MRR in 4 months with a SUPER BORING S*IT.

the reason was always the same 5 decisions.

after 50+ builds at DreamLaunch and studying multiple startups, none of it was revolutionary. no growth hacks. no viral moments. just 5 boring decisions made correctly.

1. which problem you pick. not the most exciting problem. the most painful one. if people won't pay before you build, you don't have a product, you have a hobby

2. one distribution channel picked and stuck to. not five. one. AI UGC on TikTok, reddit posts in niche communities, or an AEO-first content approach. boring, repetitive, consistent. that's it

3. pricing set correctly in week 1 and never touched again. one-time $5 vs $29/month changes your entire trajectory. most founders set it too low and never recover because they're scared to charge what the thing is worth

4. adding a weekly plan. the most unsexy pricing decision nobody talks about. monthly and yearly alone creates commitment fear. weekly converts the users who just want to test. we've seen this add 30-40% to conversion on its own

5. shipping fixes within 48 hours of hearing a complaint. not planning a roadmap. not scheduling a sprint. just fixing the thing and telling the user it's done

no AI breakthrough. no viral campaign. no secret distribution channel.

just 5 boring decisions made right while everyone else was looking for something more interesting.

get these right and everything else is just execution noise.

author: CryptooGG_
text:
HOW TO USE AI TO MAKE YOUR WORKFLOW 10X EASIER 😭

Most people use AI as a faster Google.
That’s useful.

But the bigger opportunity is using AI to connect different parts of your workflow.

Think of it like this:

INPUT → AI → TOOLS → VERIFICATION → OUTPUT

For example, imagine you’re researching a Web3 project.

You could spend 3–4 hours manually collecting everything.

Or build a workflow.

1. COLLECT

Start with sources:

→ Project docs
→ X
→ GitHub
→ DefiLlama
→ Dune
→ Token Terminal
→ News
→ Research reports

Use AI to help collect and organize the information.

But don’t treat AI as the source of truth.

2. PROCESS

Feed the information into an AI model.

Ask it to:

→ Extract key metrics
→ Identify competitors
→ Compare tokenomics
→ Summarize documentation
→ Find inconsistencies
→ Identify missing information
→ Generate questions for further research

Now you’re not just asking AI for an answer.

You’re giving it a research job.

3. VERIFY

This is the step people skip.

AI can produce a perfect-looking answer that is completely wrong.

Verify important claims against primary sources.

If AI says revenue is $5M, check the actual data.

If it says a token unlock is next month, check the official unlock schedule.

If it claims a partnership exists, find the announcement.

AI speeds up research.
It doesn’t replace verification.

4. CONNECT YOUR TOOLS

This is where automation becomes powerful.

Use tools like:

n8n
Make
Zapier

to connect your apps.

Example:

New article → AI reads it → extracts important information → summarizes it → saves it to Notion → tags the topic → adds it to your research database.

You don’t have to repeat the same 10 steps every time.

5. TURN RESEARCH INTO CONTENT

Once your research is verified:

AI can turn the same information into different formats.

One research document can become:

→ X post
→ Long-form article
→ Newsletter
→ Video script
→ Content ideas
→ Research summary

You create the knowledge once.
Then reuse it.

6. KEEP HUMANS IN THE LOOP

Don’t automate everything.

Automate repetitive tasks.

Keep judgment-heavy tasks for yourself.

AI can collect.
AI can summarize.
AI can compare.
AI can organize.
AI can draft.

But you should still decide:

What matters?
Is this actually true?
Is this worth publishing?
What’s the right conclusion?

That’s where your advantage comes from.

The future isn’t people who simply know how to prompt AI.

It’s people who can build systems around AI.

One model won’t give you an unfair advantage.

A workflow that combines:

AI + data + tools + automation + human judgment can.

Stop asking:
What’s the best AI tool?

Start asking:
What repetitive process can I turn into a system?

That’s where the real thing is !

text:
$NBIS @TolokaAI 
Shopify + Toloka: The Ground-Truth Flywheel Is Becoming the Moat for AI Agents

The next phase of AI competition will not only be about who builds the biggest model. It will be about who can build the strongest learning loop.

Shopify and Toloka’s work on Sidekick demonstrates a critical shift in AI development: production feedback infrastructure is becoming as important as model architecture.

AI agents are moving from simple chatbots into systems that execute real business tasks. Shopify’s Sidekick uses a planner model that routes merchant requests to specialized skill agents for analytics, workflows, app creation, and other tasks.

The challenge is that agents often fail silently.

They do not crash. They produce answers that look correct but subtly miss the user’s intent:

selecting the wrong database tool,
misunderstanding time periods,
generating incomplete workflows,
refusing tasks they could complete.

These failures are difficult to catch with traditional benchmarks because they only appear in messy real-world interactions.

Shopify’s solution was to create a ground-truth flywheel.

Production conversations are evaluated by AI judges. When the system detects failures, human experts review and correct the responses. Those corrections become high-quality training data used to improve both the skill agents and the evaluation models.

The loop becomes:

User interaction → AI evaluation → Human correction → Training data → Better agent → More reliable evaluation

This creates a compounding advantage.

A key lesson is that the judge itself becomes a product. If an AI system cannot accurately measure its own performance, it cannot improve reliably. A weak evaluator creates a dangerous outcome: models become better at producing convincing mistakes.

Toloka’s human annotation pipeline helps solve this by creating trusted "golden datasets" containing:

correct examples,
failure cases,
edge scenarios,
product-specific quality standards.

These datasets become the foundation for fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.

The results show the power of this approach. Shopify’s segmentation skill judge improved from 75% accuracy to 89% accuracy within one month, even before retraining the underlying model. The improvement came from better evaluation alignment and clearer failure analysis.

The system also revealed specific problems engineers could fix:

Incorrect tool selection
The agent sometimes routed requests to the wrong capability.
Unnecessary opt-outs
The agent declined tasks it was capable of completing.

Instead of blindly improving the model, Shopify could target the exact weaknesses hurting user experience.
The broader AI industry implication is significant.

Foundation models are increasingly becoming commoditized. Many companies will have access to powerful reasoning models. The differentiator will become:

proprietary user data,
evaluation systems,
feedback loops,
domain-specific training.

The future AI stack may look less like a single giant model and more like an intelligent factory:

Users generate data → evaluation identifies failures → humans provide corrections → models improve → better agents attract more users.

This is the same type of compounding advantage that powered search engines, recommendation systems, and social platforms.

The winners in the AI agent era may not simply be the companies with the smartest models.

They may be the companies that learn the fastest.

author: forgottenwildc
text:
AI Has Hit Its 20s: Time to Get a Job

For the last few years, AI has been the kid everybody bragged about.

“Look what it can draw.”

“Look what it can write.”

“Look, it passed another test.”

We stood around like proud parents while it showed off at the dinner table.

That was fine when AI was five years old.

But AI has hit its 20s now.

It is time to get a job and start paying some bills.

And that appears to be exactly where the industry is headed.

For the last several days, there really has not been some earth-shattering new model announcement every morning. Instead, companies like OpenAI are talking more and more about something far less glamorous:

How much useful work can this thing actually do for the money?

That may turn out to be a much bigger story.

OpenAI’s newest GPT-5.6 family is being pitched heavily around price-performance, not simply raw intelligence. The company says its smaller Luna model can now deliver performance comparable to models that were frontier-class roughly a year ago at about six cents on the dollar per task, while operating nearly nine times faster in OpenAI’s testing.[1]

That is a dramatic change.

A business owner does not really care whether his AI scored 3% higher on some benchmark nobody outside Silicon Valley has ever heard of.

He cares whether it can answer customers, research inventory, analyze paperwork, write listings, check records, prepare reports or handle repetitive office work — and whether doing that saves more money than it costs.

That is adulthood.

The Allowance Is Getting Cut

OpenAI recently dropped the API price of GPT-5.6 Luna to 20 cents per million input tokens and $1.20 per million output tokens. Terra now costs $2 per million input tokens and $12 per million output tokens.[2]

Those numbers sound like computer gobbledygook until you understand what is happening underneath them.

AI work is getting cheap.

Really cheap.

And that changes everything.

There are plenty of tasks where paying an employee $20 or $30 an hour made sense, but paying an AI agent several dollars every time it performed the task did not.

Cut that AI cost by 80%, and suddenly the math changes.

Do that again next year and the math changes again.

The important AI race may therefore no longer be:

Who can build the smartest machine?

It may increasingly become:

Who can build the cheapest competent worker?

And Now the Kid Can Use Tools

AI is also moving beyond sitting there waiting for somebody to ask it a question.

OpenAI’s current developer guidance spends a lot of time discussing agents, programmatic tool use and multi-agent systems.[3]

That is important.

A chatbot tells you how to do something.

An agent does it.

The difference is enormous.

Imagine telling an AI:

“Go through these 5,000 products, find the ones with weak titles, compare them with current search behavior, rewrite the listings that need help and flag anything you are unsure about.”

That is different from asking ChatGPT to rewrite one title.

Or:

“Review yesterday’s sales, compare them with the previous 90 days, separate seasonal changes from unusual changes and tell me what inventory I should concentrate on today.”

Again, that is not a chatbot.

That is work.

For businesses, this is where AI starts earning its supper.

It Doesn't Need to Be Einstein Every Minute

There is another very practical lesson emerging.

A company probably does not need the smartest AI model on Earth performing every task.

You do not hire a neurosurgeon to alphabetize the filing cabinet.

OpenAI itself now talks about matching different levels of intelligence to different portions of a workflow.

A powerful model such as Sol might examine a complicated problem and determine what should be done. A much cheaper Luna model can then carry out the routine parts — writing tests, processing documents or following well-defined instructions.[1]

That is how businesses already operate with people.

The experienced manager makes the difficult decision.

The junior employee handles the routine work.

AI is beginning to develop the same labor hierarchy.

And that might be one of the biggest reasons its economics suddenly become attractive.

The Real Breakthrough May Be Efficiency

There is another wrinkle here that matters enormously to the data-center debate.

Everyone looks at today's AI power consumption and draws a ruler straight into the future.

More AI equals more chips.

More chips equal more data centers.

More data centers equal more electricity.

Except technology does not generally work that way.

OpenAI says GPT-5.6 has already been used to improve parts of the software that run GPT-5.6 itself, helping reduce serving costs and improve token-generation efficiency.[4]

The company describes its broader strategy very plainly: get more useful work from the same amount of compute.[1]

That does not mean data centers disappear.

Far from it.

AI demand could grow so rapidly that efficiency improvements are swallowed up by increased use.

But it does mean a data center built in 2030 may produce vastly more useful work per megawatt than one built today.

That matters when people casually project today's AI infrastructure needs 10 or 20 years into the future.

They are assuming the 20-year-old AI worker will never learn how to work faster.

History suggests otherwise.

This Is Where AI Starts Getting Interesting

The gee-whiz phase of AI was entertaining.

Pictures were fun.

Poems were fun.

Watching it pass professional exams was impressive.

But none of that necessarily justified trillions of dollars of investment.

Productive labor might.

If AI agents can reliably perform useful business tasks for pennies or a few dollars, the addressable market becomes enormous.

Accounting departments.

Customer service.

Programming.

Research.

Sales.

Inventory management.

Marketing.

Legal document review.

Scheduling.

Procurement.

Data analysis.

Small-business administration.

The boring stuff is where the money lives.

That is true of most technology.

Nobody built the modern economy because computers could play chess.

Computers became indispensable because they handled payroll, inventory, banking, communications, engineering and millions of other everyday jobs.

AI appears to be reaching that stage.

Welcome to the Workforce

So perhaps the quiet period in new AI models is not a slowdown at all.

Maybe AI is simply growing up.

The industry's attention is shifting from:

“Look how smart it is.”

to:

“What can it do, how fast can it do it, and what does it cost me?”

That is a much healthier question.

AI has spent several years being the brilliant child everybody wanted to show off.

Now it is standing in the kitchen, 20 years old, eating everything in the refrigerator.

At some point Dad has to point toward the front door and say:

“You're very impressive. Now go get a job.”

Judging from the direction OpenAI and the rest of the industry are heading, AI may finally be doing exactly that.

Footnotes

[1] OpenAI, “Advancing the price-performance frontier with GPT-5.6,” July 30, 2026. OpenAI says GPT-5.6 Luna delivers performance comparable to models that were frontier-class a year earlier at roughly six cents on the dollar per task and discusses assigning different models to different stages of business workflows. (OpenAI)

[2] OpenAI, GPT-5.6 pricing / ChatGPT Enterprise Rate Card. Current listed prices include Luna at $0.20 per million input tokens and $1.20 per million output tokens, with Terra at $2 and $12 respectively. (OpenAI Help Center)

[3] OpenAI, “The builder’s guide to GPT-5.6,” August 13, 2026. OpenAI focuses on production agents, programmatic tool calling, multi-agent workflows, prompt caching and reducing the cost of frontier-level agent performance. (OpenAI)

[4] OpenAI, “How GPT-5.6 fuses frontier intelligence with frontier efficiency,” July 29, 2026. OpenAI details improvements in inference, context handling and agent efficiency intended to produce more useful work from available compute. (OpenAI)

#AI #ArtificialIntelligence #AIAgents #OpenAI #SmallBusiness #Technology #FutureOfWork #Automation

author: arevmarkos
text:
🤖 The biggest mistake people make with AI agents?

They start with the model.

“Which LLM should I use?”

GPT? Claude? Gemini? Grok?

That's often the wrong first question.

If you're building an AI agent that is supposed to do real work, the model is only one component of the system.

Think about what happens when you give an agent access to a real environment.

A server.
An API.
A database.
A cloud platform.
Production logs.
Suddenly, generating a good answer isn't enough.
The agent needs to understand the environment, make a decision, execute an action and verify what happened.
That's where things get interesting.
A practical AI agent might need:

🧠 Reasoning

Understand the problem and decide what to do.

🔌 Tools

APIs, SSH, databases, cloud platforms and other systems it can interact with.

📚 Context

Documentation, logs, configuration and historical information.

⚙️ Execution

The ability to actually perform an approved action instead of simply describing it.

🔍 Verification

Check whether the action solved the problem or created another one.

🛡️ Guardrails

Permissions, limits, approvals and isolation so one bad decision doesn't become a production incident.

📊 Observability

Logs and metrics that allow us to understand what the agent actually did.

And this changes the architecture completely.

Instead of:

User → Chatbot → Answer

we're moving toward:

Event → Context → Agent → Tools → Action → Verification → Result

The difficult part isn't making the AI say something intelligent.

The difficult part is making it reliable when the real world doesn't behave like the prompt.

What happens when an API times out?

What happens when a command returns an unexpected result?

What happens when the agent misunderstands the state of the system?

What happens when the “correct” action is potentially destructive?

That's where I think the next generation of AI engineering will be won.

Not by who has the most impressive demo.

But by who can build systems that are useful, observable, controllable and reliable.

I'm going to start building and testing these systems in real environments and document what works, what fails, and why.

AI × Automation × Infrastructure

No hype.
Just engineering.

author: CoachOxlade_
text:
TECHNICAL TUESDAY ⚙️

Are businesses actually ready for the AI they keep saying they want?

We keep asking:

“How can my business use AI?”

But maybe we’re asking the wrong question.

Because AI isn’t one technology.

A chatbot answering customers is AI.

A system predicting demand is AI.

Google Maps recommending a route is AI.

An AI Agent making decisions and taking actions is AI.

They all require very different things.

And this is where it gets interesting.

You can give a company the most powerful AI model available and still get terrible results if:

The data is messy.

The systems don’t communicate.

Nobody knows who is responsible when AI makes a mistake.

The employees don’t understand how to use it.

Or the company hasn’t identified the actual problem it’s trying to solve.

The technology might be ready.

The organization might not be.

That’s why I think the next phase of AI won’t simply be about who has access to the most powerful models.

It will be about who can build the right systems around them.

So here’s my question:

If you were responsible for introducing AI into a company tomorrow, what would you fix first: the technology, the data, the people, or the workflow?

I want to hear your reasoning.

Build. Solve. Scale.

author: applekhankorea
text:
Strategic Predictive Analysis :::
The Turning Point for Pi App Studio — From the Democratization of App Creation to a Real-Utility Transaction Economy
( https://t.co/vThnI3XN85 )

[[[ This article includes Predictive & Technical Analysis  and may differ from actual outcomes ]]]
[[[ The End of Indiscriminate AI Subsidies — Shifting Resources Toward Creators Who Generate Real Utility Rather Than Simply Increasing the Number of Apps ]]]
[[[ From Real Users to Real Transactions — Why Distinct Users and Repeat Usage May Become Leading Indicators of Community-Level Economic Activity ]]]
[[[ Transaction Engines Backed by Real Goods and Services — The Most Important Future Apps May Be Those That Generate the Greatest Volume of Meaningful Economic Activity ]]]
[[[ From App Studio to Launchpad and Distributed Compute — How Utility-Weighted Resource Allocation Could Expand Into a Unified Productive Economic System ]]]

-----------------------------------------
Introduction — This Announcement Is More Than a Simple Price Increase
-----------------------------------------
Beginning on August 24, 2026, Pi App Studio will change the way app creation and editing are priced.

On the surface, the change appears straightforward. Until now, creators paid 0.25 Pi to create an app and 0.25 Pi to edit one. Under the new model, the standard price will move closer to the actual cost of the AI services required to create or modify an application.

However, a closer reading of the announcement suggests that the real significance of the change lies not in the price itself.

Pi Network explains that during the initial period of App Studio, it heavily subsidized the cost of AI-powered creation for all creators. This allowed the platform to observe how creators used App Studio, which apps attracted real users, and which applications had the potential to develop genuine utility.

Pi now states that it has accumulated enough data from this introductory period to begin allocating subsidies selectively.

In other words, the system appears to be moving through the following progression:

App Creation Democratization
↓
Creator Behavior Observation
↓
Real User Measurement
↓
Utility Evaluation
↓
Selective AI Resource Subsidy

This is therefore not merely a pricing adjustment.
It may represent the beginning of a transition in which Pi App Studio evolves from an experimental environment where anyone can create applications into a mechanism that increasingly identifies and supports creators capable of building actual product economies.
And once this transition is extended strategically, the central competitive question may eventually become:
Who can connect the greatest amount of real goods and services to the community and, as a result, continuously generate the largest volume of meaningful economic transactions?
That may be the most important strategic direction implied by this change.

-----
1. The End of Indiscriminate AI Subsidies
Shifting Resources Toward Creators Who Generate Real Utility Rather Than Simply Increasing the Number of Apps
The initial pricing model of Pi App Studio had an obvious purpose.
By reducing the cost of AI-assisted application development to an extremely low level, Pi enabled even Pioneers without conventional software-development experience to experiment with building applications.

As a result, App Studio effectively became a large-scale experimentation environment.

If someone had an idea, they could create an application. If they wanted to modify it, they could repeatedly iterate at very little cost.

During this stage, participation itself mattered more than efficiency.

But such a model inevitably creates another problem.

If app creation is almost free, the same subsidy is consumed not only by applications attempting to solve real problems, but also by:

experimental apps, personal test apps, duplicate applications, one-time projects, meaningless repetitive generation, and spam-like applications.

Pi explicitly addresses this issue in the announcement.

Continuing to subsidize every creation equally would result in a substantial amount of resources being consumed by the long tail of applications created only for testing, experimentation, or spam.

The essence of the new policy can therefore be summarized as follows:

Everyone may still build.But:Not everyone will continue receiving the same level of subsidy.

The opportunity to enter remains open, while continued network support increasingly becomes concentrated on creators who demonstrate actual utility.

This is an important transition.

The earlier criterion was largely:

Creation

whereas the new criterion increasingly becomes:

Contribution

And the first objective signal Pi has selected for evaluating that contribution is the presence of distinct real users.

A creator using their own application is not enough.

Other people must actually use it.

The economic unit of evaluation therefore begins shifting from:
“An app exists.”
to:
“Other people genuinely find this app useful.”
Strategically, this can be described as:

Utility-Weighted Resource Allocation

The network's AI resources are no longer subsidized indiscriminately. Instead, more favorable resource economics are directed toward creators who demonstrate meaningful utility.

-----
2. From Real Users to Real Transactions

Why Distinct Users and Repeat Usage May Become Leading Indicators of Community-Level Economic Activity

An important distinction must be maintained here.

The current App Studio announcement does not state that subsidy eligibility will be determined directly by transaction volume.

The explicitly stated criteria relate to:

real users, distinct users, usage by people other than the creator, and demonstrated utility.

Therefore, it would be premature to say:

“Pi is now ranking apps according to transaction count.”

That is not what has been announced.

However, when considering the strategic evolution of the ecosystem, the next question becomes relatively natural.

Pi App Studio is not merely a generic content-creation platform. It is intended to help build applications within an economic ecosystem.

Once an application acquires genuine users and sustained usage, the next question becomes:

“What are those users actually doing inside the application?”

When utility applications begin performing real economic functions, activities such as the following naturally emerge:

Purchasing goods
Ordering food
Requesting delivery
Booking accommodation
Purchasing digital services
Requesting AI services
Hiring professional services
Consuming compute
Consuming storage
Exchanging physical goods between individuals

Each of these activities is backed by an actual product or service.

They are fundamentally different from simple app clicks.

And each utility event can generate one or more economic transactions.

Therefore, the long-term development path could look like this:

Distinct Users
↓
Retention
↓
Repeated Utility
↓
Real Goods & Services
↓
Meaningful Transactions
↓
Community Economic Throughput

The critical concept here is not raw transaction count.

A million transfers of 0.000001 Pi between accounts do not represent a million units of genuine utility.

Therefore, if the evaluation framework eventually becomes more sophisticated, the relevant target should not simply be:

Transactions / Day

but something closer to:

Meaningful Economic Transactions

or:

Verified Economic Utility

The strongest applications will not merely make the network busy.

They will solve real human needs while naturally generating genuine economic activity.

-----
3. Transaction Engines Backed by Real Goods and Services
The Most Important Future Apps May Be Those That Generate the Greatest Volume of Meaningful Economic Activity
At this point, the competitive logic of the Pi application ecosystem begins to change substantially.
The first stage of competition was:
Who can build an app?
The next stage becomes:
Who can attract real users?
But in a mature economic ecosystem, the ultimate competition may become:
Who can connect the greatest amount of real goods and services to the largest number of users and, as a result, generate the greatest amount of recurring economic activity?

Such an application can be described as a:

Real-Utility Transaction Engine

Consider a hypothetical lifestyle utility application used by one million people.

Suppose one user performs, on average:

one food purchase, two transportation transactions, five AI service interactions, and two content purchases per day.
That would produce ten meaningful economic events per user per day.
Across one million users:
1,000,000 Users × 10 Economic Events= 10,000,000 Meaningful Economic Events per Day
And these are not merely payments.
A single food order may involve:
Restaurant
Ordering system
Payment
Delivery
Location services
Data storage
Compute
Thus:
1 Human Utility Event→ N Infrastructure Events
The expansion becomes even greater once AI agents participate.
A human may issue only one instruction:

“Prepare dinner for me tonight.”

Yet the AI agent may subsequently perform:

price comparison, product discovery, grocery purchasing, delivery scheduling, payment, compute calls, and calendar coordination.

The result becomes:

1 Human Intent
↓
N Agent Tasks
↓
M Services
↓
K Economic Transactions

This may become one of the defining features of the AI-agent economy.

The number of machine-level economic events created by AI agents acting on behalf of humans may eventually become far larger than the number of transactions humans initiate manually.

Under such conditions, the competitiveness of a future Pi application may depend less on how visually impressive the interface is and more on:

How many real economic intentions can the application successfully execute?

At that point, an application is no longer merely software.

It becomes:

Community Economic Infrastructure

-----
4. From App Studio to Launchpad and Distributed Compute

How Utility-Weighted Resource Allocation Could Expand Into a Unified Productive Economic System

From this point onward, the analysis moves beyond what is directly stated in the announcement and enters the territory of strategic prediction based on currently observable directions.

The most important economic principle in the new App Studio policy is:

Scarce AI resources should not be subsidized equally for every creator.More resources should be directed toward creators who demonstrate actual utility.

There is no technical reason why such a principle would have to remain limited to App Studio.

If Pi eventually expands distributed compute, storage, AI inference, and related resource markets, the same philosophy could theoretically be applied there as well.

For example:

No demonstrated users
→ Standard compute pricingDemonstrated utility
→ Compute subsidyLarge-scale community utility
→ Higher resource tier

Pi has not announced such a compute-subsidy hierarchy.

However, the new App Studio model may provide an early economic example of what a broader resource-allocation philosophy could eventually look like.

This direction also aligns with the product-first philosophy associated with Launchpad.

An ideal progression could be:

Idea
↓
App Studio
↓
Working Product
↓
Real Users
↓
Repeated Utility
↓
Real Economic Transactions
↓
Product Economy
↓
Launchpad / Tokenization

In other words, tokens would not create the economy first.

Instead:
An economy would already exist, and tokenization would be added afterward.
This reverses the conventional cryptocurrency sequence:

Token → Fundraising → Product

into something closer to:

Problem → Product → Users → Utility → Transactions → Token
If this structure is successfully implemented, the strongest Launchpad projects would not necessarily be those with the largest communities or the loudest marketing.
The strongest projects could instead be those that already possess:
real users,
real products,
real services,
recurring usage,
and real transactions.

-----
5. Why the “No Markup” Statement Matters
One particularly interesting sentence appears in the announcement.
Pi states that while standard pricing will more closely reflect the actual underlying AI service cost:

Pi will not add any markup to the underlying AI service costs.

This is economically significant.
Rather than maximizing platform margins from AI-generation fees, Pi appears to be positioning App Studio primarily as infrastructure for enabling creators to build useful products.
Conceptually, the structure becomes:

For an ordinary creator:

Actual AI Cost ≈ Creator Price

For a creator who demonstrates utility:

Actual AI Cost − Network Subsidy

This suggests that the economic objective is not necessarily:

Maximizing AI-tool revenue

but rather:
Maximizing Useful Application Production
If the same logic were eventually extended to distributed compute, the implications would become even more interesting.
Instead of maximizing margins on each compute unit, the system could theoretically pursue:
Compute Price ↓↓↓Utility Apps ↑↑Agent Activity ↑↑Economic Transactions ↑↑Network Throughput ↑↑
The strategy would therefore shift away from extracting high margins from individual services and toward maximizing the total volume of economic activity across the network.

-----
6. “The Most Transactions” Must Always Come With One Condition

The most important safeguard in this entire analysis is:

Transaction Count ≠ Utility

If developers were rewarded purely according to transaction volume, they would quickly learn how to manipulate the number.

A sophisticated future economic evaluation system would therefore need something more nuanced than raw TPS.

Conceptually, one could imagine a metric such as:

Economic Utility Density
= Meaningful Goods & Service Activity / Resources Consumed

This could incorporate factors such as:

Distinct Humans
Retention
Real Product or Service
Repeat Transactions
Transaction Diversity
Economic Value
Resource Efficiency

Under such a framework, one million spam transactions could be worth less than one hundred thousand genuine delivery, commerce, AI-service, or professional-service transactions.

This distinction is essential.

What the network should reward is not:

Block Space Consumption

but:
Economic Utility Creation

-----
7. App Studio Could Eventually Become a Creator Selection Engine

Another important aspect of the new policy is that eligibility is not a one-time decision.

Pi states that subsidy qualification will be reviewed continuously as new data is generated.

A creator who does not qualify today may later qualify after attracting more genuine users.

If this logic continues to mature, the system may gradually evolve away from a static concept such as:
Certified Developer
toward something closer to:
Dynamic Utility Reputation
Imagine that App Studio eventually accumulates data such as:
Creator A
3 apps
200,000 unique users
High retention
Repeated goods-and-services transactionsCreator B
150 apps
400 unique users
Almost no sustained usage
By raw app count, Creator B appears much more active.
By actual economic contribution, Creator A is overwhelmingly stronger.

Once data of this kind accumulates over time, the creator themselves may acquire a kind of:

Utility Reputation

And such reputation could theoretically become relevant to future opportunities involving AI resources, Launchpad access, compute resources, or other ecosystem functions.

No such broader integration has been officially announced.

However, the new App Studio policy already introduces two foundational components required for such a system:
measurable user data
and dynamic re-evaluation.

-----
8. Ultimately, the Competition Is Not Between Apps — It Is Between Economic Networks
In the early days of Pi App Studio:
one app
was simply one product.
But once a genuine utility application grows, it begins to contain:
users, merchants, suppliers, service providers, AI agents, compute providers, storage providers, and payment flows.
At that point, the application begins to resemble a small economy.
A marketplace application, for example, may connect:
Sellers
Buyers
Logistics
Payments
Customer support
AI recommendations
Advertising
Data infrastructure
The real competition among creators therefore shifts from:
Who can design the best-looking interface?
to:
Who can connect the largest number of economic actors inside their utility network?

This represents a profound change.

In the traditional app economy, developers often focus on:

Monthly Active Users

But inside an economic ecosystem such as Pi, a more meaningful long-term metric could become:

Monthly Active Economic Users

And beyond that:

Economic Events per Active User

Ultimately:

User Count × Utility Frequency × Economic Events

could become a far more useful measure of the economic significance of an application.

-----
9. Strategic Final Prediction — Pi May Be Moving From Maximizing the Number of Apps to Maximizing the Density of Economic Activity
The new announcement can be compressed into one strategic interpretation.
The original purpose of App Studio was to maximize:
Creation Density

Anyone could create an application.

Now the objective appears to be shifting toward:

Utility Density

Applications that people actually use receive stronger support.

The next natural stage could become:

Economic Activity Density

At that point, what matters is how much real exchange of goods and services occurs.

The evolutionary sequence could therefore be described as:

Creation Density
↓
User Density
↓
Utility Density
↓
Transaction Density
↓
Economic Throughput

The first part of this progression is already directly supported by the new App Studio announcement.

The later stages—Transaction Density and Economic Throughput—remain strategic predictions based on the economic direction of the system.

But if Pi intends to mature into a genuine commercial ecosystem, those stages would be difficult to avoid.

An economy does not exist because many apps have been created.

An economy exists when:

real goods and services are repeatedly exchanged.

---------------------------------------------
Conclusion — The Most Important Future Pi Apps May Not Be the Apps People Look At, but the Apps That Move the Economy
---------------------------------------------
The App Studio pricing change contains much more than a simple adjustment to AI-generation costs.

Pi first gave all creators access to an extremely inexpensive AI-powered development environment.

That phase generated large amounts of experimentation data.
Now the network is beginning to concentrate subsidies on creators whose applications attract genuine users and demonstrate real utility.
This represents a transition from:
Quantity → Quality
But quality may not be the final stage.
Beyond quality lies:
Economic Utility
And the strongest expression of economic utility is ultimately:
Repeated community-level transactions backed by real goods and services

Therefore, the central competitive question for the future Pi application ecosystem may be summarized as follows:

“Not who can build the greatest number of apps, but who can continuously connect the greatest number of community members to real goods and services and, as a result, generate the largest number of meaningful economic transactions.”

An application capable of doing that is no longer simply a utility app.

It becomes a:

Real-Utility Transaction Engine

and, at the same time:

Community Economic Infrastructure

If thousands of such applications eventually emerge, and if Personal AI Agents, Distributed Compute, Storage, Wallets, and Payments increasingly operate behind them, the fundamental unit used to measure the Pi economy itself could begin to change:

Apps → Users → Utility → Transactions → Economic Throughput
And in an AI-agent economy, the structure could evolve even further:

1 Human Intent → N Agent Actions → M Services → K Economic Transactions

From that perspective, the August 2026 App Studio pricing policy may prove to be more than a small pricing adjustment.
It could represent an early signal that Pi's application ecosystem is moving beyond the era of indiscriminate creation and entering an era in which real economic utility begins to determine how network resources are allocated.
The competitive principle then becomes remarkably simple:
Build less noise.
Create real utility.
Generate real economic activity.
Ultimately, where real goods and services exist, transactions follow; and where those transactions repeat, an economy emerges.
The latest Pi App Studio policy change may be an early indication that ecosystem resources are beginning to be reorganized around precisely that principle.
